text:
In the last video, you saw why a final response isn't always enough to
tell whether an agent completed a task correctly.

Sometimes, the failure happens earlier, in one of the actions the
agent takes along the way.

So the next question is, when an agent takes an action,
what exactly should you evaluate? Let's start with the dog shelter.

Suppose a volunteer says, "I can't make Saturday anymore.
Please cancel my outing."

The agent looks up the booking, but instead of canceling it,
it confirms the outing. The booking details might all be correct.

It may have found the right volunteer, the right dog, and the right
date. None of that matters if the agent chose the wrong action.
The volunteer asked to cancel, but the agent decided to confirm.

So one thing you need to evaluate is simply, did the agent choose the
right action for the request? Now consider a different example.
A volunteer says, "Can you book me with Pepper on Friday at 5:30?"

The agent creates a booking, so this time it chose the
right kind of action.

But when you inspect the booking, it scheduled Saturday at 5:30.
That's a different failure.

The agent knew it needed to create a booking,
it just carried that action out with the wrong details.

So there are really two separate questions here:
What action did the agent decide to take?
And once it made that choice, did it execute the action correctly?

Keeping those questions separate becomes especially useful
when the action itself has several parameters,

because an agent can make the right decision and still pass the wrong
information into the action.

There are a couple of other cases that you need to watch for, too.
Sometimes the problem is that a required action never happens.

For example, the shelter requires an eligibility check before any
outing can be booked.

If the agent goes straight from the volunteer's request to creating
the booking, action itself might be perfectly formed,
but a required action is missing from the process.

And sometimes the agent takes an action that should not happen at all.
Suppose a volunteer asks, "Can I take Pepper home permanently?"

The shelter agent is designed to schedule outings.
It doesn't have the authority to approve an adoption.

So if it creates some kind of permanent placement or treats the
request like a normal booking,

the failure is not that the action was executed badly;
the action should never have been taken in the first place.

When you evaluate actions, you need to check all of these situations.
Did the agent choose the right action?

Did it carry it out with the right details? Did it skip something
required? Or did it do something it shouldn't have done?

Now, let's translate that into Northwind. For the Northwind agent,
actions are tool calls. If a customer asks, "Where is order 4521?"

the agent may need to call an order lookup tool.
So the first question is whether it chose the right tool.

If it calls a product search tool instead,
that's an action selection failure.

The tool may work perfectly, but it's the wrong operation for
the customer's request.

If it does choose the order lookup tool, there's still a second
question: did it call the tool with the right arguments?

Suppose the customer asked about order 4521,
but the agent calls order_lookup(order_id="4512").

That's a subtle failure because 4512 might also be a real order,
The tool can run successfully and return valid-looking information,

and the agent may then give the customer a perfectly fluent answer
about the wrong order.
So checking whether the tool call succeeded is not enough.

You need to compare the arguments the agent used with the information
it was supposed to act on.

You'll often see these two checks described as tool selection
and tool invocation.
Tool selection asks whether the agent chose the correct tool.

invocation asks whether it called that tool correctly,
including the arguments it passed.

And just like in the shelter example, you also need to consider cases
where a tool should be required or prohibited.
Suppose a customer asks for the status of an order.

If the agent answers without ever calling order lookup, that may be a
problem if the status has to come from the current order system.

In that case, you can check that the required tool actually
appeared in the trace.

Now imagine a customer asks for a refund,
but the order is outside Northwind's refund window.

If policy says the refund cannot be processed,
then process_refund should not appear at all.

So a useful evaluator sometimes checks for the presence of a tool call
and sometimes checks for its absence.

There's another important case where the agent doesn't yet have
enough information to act.

Suppose the customer says, "Can you refund my purchase?" but there's
no order number and no other way to identify which purchase they mean.

Before you evaluate the agent, you need to define what the
correct behavior should be.

Maybe Northwind's policy says the agent should ask which order the
customer wants refunded before doing anything else.
Once that expectation is clear,

you can check whether the agent asked for the missing information
rather than guessing or calling the refund tool prematurely.

This is a small example of something you've been doing throughout the
course, Before you can evaluate a behavior,
you need to know what counts as correct.

Once that's defined, the trace gives you the evidence to check it.
And tool calls have an advantage here.

A lot of that evidence is structured, You can inspect the tool name
and the arguments directly.

You can check whether a required tool appeared,
whether a forbidden tool appeared,

or whether the order_id passed into the call matches the order the
customer actually asked about.

When the thing you care about is represented explicitly in the trace,
a simple deterministic check is often enough.

You don't need an LLM judge to tell you that 4521 and 4512 are
different order IDs.

But even if every individual tool call looks correct,
the run can still fail.

Suppose Northwind calls the right inventory tool with the right
product ID, and the tool returns that the item is out of stock,
then the agent tells the customer, "Yes, it's available."

tool selection passed, tool invocation passed,
but the final result is still wrong.

Or imagine several individually valid tool calls happen in the wrong
order. That gives you the next evaluation problem.

In the next video, you'll stop looking at actions one at a time
and evaluate the trajectory,

the sequence of steps the agent took through the task,
what each step returned, and how those steps fit together.
